topic.title: Motor Learning and Adaptive Embodied Control
topic.overview: Motor learning connects desired movements with the dynamics of a body and its actuators. The represented work learns inverse dynamics, reusable movement primitives, adaptation to morphology, and low-dimensional coordination of many actuators. Physical continuity and body structure can make the learning problem easier than an unconstrained search over actions.
topic.whyItMatters: A controller must remain effective when speed, load, or body configuration changes. Useful representations can reduce the experience needed to learn coordinated behavior while retaining the ability to produce precise movements.
topic.evolution: An early 1987 robot learns visual–joint mappings through action, and a 1992 practice strategy gradually increases trajectory difficulty. Later work studies attractor-based primitives and character control; recent methods emphasize morphological attention and actuator coordination. These examples share the use of structured representations, without implying that modern control guarantees apply to the earlier systems.
openQuestions: Which action representations transfer across changes in mechanical structure?
How can learned coordination retain control authority during unexpected contact?
